subtopics.title: Refugee, Asylum Seeker and Migrant
subtopics.summary: The booklet distinguishes three categories of people on the move: refugees, asylum seekers and migrants. Each category differs in why the person moves, what protection applies, and which law governs the person's stay.
facts: Refugee: forced to flee due to persecution or conflict.
Refugee is protected under the 1951 Refugee Convention.
Refugees cannot be forcibly returned (non-refoulement).
Asylum seeker: a person seeking recognition as a refugee.
Asylum seeker is awaiting a decision on refugee status.
Asylum seeker receives temporary protection during the application.
Migrant: moves mainly for work, education or better opportunities.
Migrant may migrate legally or irregularly.
Migrant is governed mainly by domestic immigration laws.

subtopics.title: Ceuta: Location and Strategic Importance
subtopics.summary: Ceuta is an Autonomous City of Spain on the northern coast of Africa, next to Morocco. Its position at the eastern entrance of the Strait of Gibraltar makes it one of the shortest routes into European territory from Africa. Together with Melilla, it forms one of the EU's two land borders with Africa.

Ceuta lies on the northern coast of Africa.
Ceuta's neighbouring country is Morocco.
Ceuta's coast faces the Mediterranean Sea.

Ceuta represents one of the shortest routes into European territory from Africa.
Ceuta and Melilla together form one of the EU's two land borders with Africa.
Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish exclaves separated from Morocco by fortified border fences, which are often breached by immigrants.

subtopics.title: Spanish Territories and the Western Sahara Link
subtopics.summary: Ceuta, Melilla and Plazas de Soberania are Spanish territories associated with the North African mainland. Morocco disputes their status, and the migration issue is closely linked to the Western Sahara dispute. Changes in Spain's relations with Morocco and Algeria have repeatedly affected migration flows through Ceuta.

subtopics.title: International Frameworks on Refugees and Trafficking
subtopics.summary: Several international instruments govern refugees and human trafficking. The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol set out refugee protection, while the Palermo instruments of 2000 target organised crime and trafficking. Other treaties and forums address refugee children, host countries and civil and political rights.
facts: The UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (Palermo Convention, 2000) combats transnational organised crime through international cooperation.
The Palermo Protocol (2000) aims to prevent, suppress and punish trafficking in persons, especially women and children.
The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as one fleeing persecution.
The 1951 Convention specifies certain categories, such as war criminals, who do not qualify for refugee status.
The 1967 Protocol expanded refugee protection beyond Europe, removing geographic and time limits.
The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) safeguards individuals from torture or inhuman treatment upon return.
The Global Compact on Refugees (2018) offers a framework to support refugees and host countries.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) advocates for refugee children's welfare.
The Global Refugee Forum is held every four years.

subtopics.title: UNHCR and India's Approach to Refugees
subtopics.summary: The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) was formed in 1950 as successor to the International Refugee Organization, and its office originated in 1921 under the League of Nations. India is not a signatory to the 1951 Convention or the 1967 Protocol, and it regulates undocumented foreigners under domestic Acts.

UNHCR succeeded the International Refugee Organization (1946).
The office of High Commissioner for Refugees originated in 1921 under the League of Nations, led by Fridtjof Nansen.
UNHCR's headquarters are in Geneva, Switzerland.
UNHCR received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
The UNHCR Nansen Refugee Award was established in 1954 and is named after Fridtjof Nansen.
The Nansen Award honours exceptional service to refugees, displaced or stateless people annually.
India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol.

All undocumented foreigners in India are regulated under the Foreigners Act (1946), the Registration of Foreigners Act (1939), the Passport (Entry into India) Act (1920) and the Citizenship Act (1955).

subtopics.title: Location and Geography of the South China Sea
subtopics.summary: The South China Sea is an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean that borders the South-East Asian mainland. It is bordered by seven countries and connects with the East China Sea and the Philippine Sea through two straits. Together with the East China Sea, it forms what is termed the China Sea.

subtopics.title: Importance of the South China Sea
subtopics.summary: The sea holds large estimated reserves of oil and natural gas and has rich fishing grounds. It is also a major trade corridor, with UNCTAD estimating that over a fifth of global trade passes through it. Nearly one-third of the world's shipping trade moves through this waterway each year.

subtopics.title: Antelope Reef Development and Strategic Role
subtopics.summary: China has completed the first phase of development at Antelope Reef, which lies in the disputed Paracel Islands. The project reportedly includes an artificial island of nearly 6 km and a 680-metre wharf linked to a deep-water harbour. China says the development serves civilian purposes, but the facility could also strengthen its military infrastructure and protect its submarines.

subtopics.title: Legal Disputes: Nine-Dash Line, UNCLOS and the PCA
subtopics.summary: China's claims in the South China Sea are described through the Nine-Dash Line, which began as an 11-dashed line in 1947. UNCLOS came into force in 1994 as a legal framework, but its interpretation in this sea remains fiercely disputed. In 2016 the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled that China's claims over 90% of the sea were illegitimate, and China rejected the ruling.

subtopics.title: Island Claims and Implications for India
subtopics.summary: The Paracel Islands are claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam, and China has exercised de facto control since 1974. The Spratly Islands and Scarborough Shoal also have overlapping claims, and a 2012 standoff gave China de facto control over the Scarborough region. For India, regional stability matters because much of its maritime commerce passes through this sea and the Malacca Strait.

topics.title: UNSC Straw Poll for Next UN Secretary-General

subtopics.title: Selection Process and Nominations
subtopics.summary: The selection begins with a joint communication from the Presidents of the General Assembly and the Security Council, inviting UN Member States to nominate candidates. Candidates typically submit a CV and vision statement, then take part in interactive dialogues with member states. Straw polls then narrow the field before the Council formally recommends a candidate.

Selection involves 2 formal stages: UNSC recommends, UNGA appoints

subtopics.title: Straw Polls and Permanent Member Signals
subtopics.summary: Straw polls are informal and confidential voting exercises that assess how acceptable each candidate is to Security Council members. Members indicate Encourage, Discourage or No Opinion. In later rounds the Permanent Members use distinctively coloured ballots, so a Discourage from a Permanent Member signals a likely veto. Rounds continue until a candidate demonstrates sufficient support.

subtopics.title: Appointment, Term and Regional Rotation
subtopics.summary: Article 97 provides for appointment by the General Assembly on the Council's recommendation, and appointments have traditionally been made by consensus or acclamation. The Charter sets no fixed term; established practice provides for a 5-year term, conventionally renewable once. Regional rotation is an informal political convention that promotes geographical representation.

Established UN practice provides for a 5-year term

subtopics.title: UNSC Structure and the Veto
subtopics.summary: The UNSC is one of the six principal organs of the UN and has 15 members, each with one vote. The five Permanent Members hold veto power, so opposition from any one of them blocks a decision regardless of wider support. The booklet argues that the Council still reflects the post-Second World War order rather than the present world.

subtopics.title: Cauvery River and its basin
subtopics.summary: The Cauvery is an east-flowing Peninsular River, known as 'Ganga of the South', that rises at Talakaveri in Kodagu, Karnataka. It flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu before draining into the Bay of Bengal near Poompuhar. Its drainage basin covers four states and UTs, and its upper and lower basins receive different monsoons.

subtopics.title: Historical roots and tribunal awards
subtopics.summary: The dispute has roots in an 1892 agreement between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore, after which Madras objected to Mysore's irrigation and storage plans. A 1924 agreement allowed Mysore to build a dam at Kannambadi, which led to the Krishnaraja Sagar Dam. After the agreement came up for review following 1974, the matter moved to the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, constituted in 1990, whose 2007 award and the 2018 Supreme Court judgment fixed the water shares.

Madras objected to Mysore's plans to expand irrigation and build storage structures

subtopics.title: Cauvery Water Management Authority
subtopics.summary: The Cauvery Water Management Authority was established in 2018 under the Cauvery Water Management Scheme, 2018, along with the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee. Its composition mixes full-time members, part-time central government members and part-time members from the basin states, with headquarters in New Delhi under the Ministry of Jal Shakti.

subtopics.title: Mekedatu project and the latest order

subtopics.title: Historical Evolution and Gorkha Identity
subtopics.summary: The Gorkhas are people of Nepali origin, and the term is linked to the historic Gorkha Kingdom of Western Nepal. Political demands for greater autonomy trace back to the early twentieth century, and they were later voiced through a 1947 memorandum seeking Gorkhasthan and the 1980s agitation led by the Gorkha National Liberation Front. Over time, the movement increasingly articulated its objective as achieving statehood within the Indian Union.

subtopics.title: Major Bases of the Demand
subtopics.summary: Supporters argue that the Darjeeling Hills population has a distinct linguistic, cultural and social identity compared with the Bengali-majority plains. Concerns over identity insecurity and racial stereotyping have strengthened demands for stronger political recognition and representation. Economic concerns cover infrastructure, employment, developmental neglect and insufficient political and fiscal autonomy.

subtopics.title: Institutional Arrangements
subtopics.summary: Two arrangements have given the hill region a measure of autonomy. The Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council, established in 1988, was constrained by limited legislative authority, inadequate financial autonomy and dependence on the state government. The Gorkhaland Territorial Administration, established in 2011, was a more empowered autonomous arrangement with greater administrative, executive and financial responsibilities.

topics.title: Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: NEET-UG 2024 leak and the 2024 Act
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Amendment follows the NEET-UG 2024 paper leak controversy, in which alleged leak networks were reported in Patna (Bihar) and Hazaribagh (Jharkhand). Investigations and Supreme Court monitoring exposed organised cheating syndicates. Parliament responded by enacting the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, which the text describes as India's first dedicated central legislation on this issue.

subtopics.title: Harsher punishments under the 2026 Amendment
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Amendment revises penalties across four categories: individual offences, service providers, organised examination crime and organised crimes. Individual offences move from 3-5 years to 5-10 years, and the service-provider ban rises from 4 years to 8 years. Organised examination crime and organised crimes also get revised minimum terms and fines.

Appeals before High Courts are heard by a two-judge bench and disposed of within a fixed period. Supreme Court precedents treat speedy trial as a fundamental right and recognise that no fixed time limit can be set for all criminal trials.

topics.title: Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: Vande Mataram: origin and early history
subtopics.summary: Vande Mataram was written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay as a patriotic response to British promotion of 'God Save the King/Queen'. It was written on 7 November 1875 in the magazine Bangadarshan and published in the novel Anandamath in 1882. It became a rallying cry of the Swadeshi Movement after the Partition of Bengal in 1905.

subtopics.title: Tribunals vs Ordinary Courts
subtopics.summary: Ordinary courts and administrative tribunals differ mainly in who controls the tenure and service conditions of their members. Civil courts have judicial authority over civil suits, while tribunals are created by statute to hear special cases defined by statutes. Impartiality is a crucial requirement for judges in a court of law.

subtopics.title: Constitutional Framework and History
subtopics.summary: Part XIV-A, inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976, contains Articles 323A and 323B, which empower Parliament and State Legislatures to set up tribunals. In L. subtopics.title: Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026 and the National Tribunals Commission
subtopics.summary: The Lok Sabha has passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026, which seeks to repeal the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and re-enact provisions that were struck down. The Bill proposes a National Tribunals Commission that gives tribunals a common institutional framework for selection, performance review, discipline and data. The Central Government must complete appointments within three months of receiving a recommendation.

The Bill re-enacts provisions of the 2021 Act that were struck down.
The National Tribunals Commission provides a Common Institutional Framework for Tribunals.

Chairpersons are capped at 70 years and Members at 67, with a maximum five-year term, whichever is earlier.
The framework covers 16 Tribunals and Authorities.
The Central Government must complete the appointment process within 3 months of receiving a recommendation.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly scrutinised provisions giving the Executive excessive control over tribunals, including in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2010-2025).

subtopics.title: National Green Tribunal
subtopics.summary: The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body set up in 2010 under the National Green Tribunal Act, with the objective of giving relief and compensation for environmental damage. It is guided by principles of natural justice and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, and its decisions can be executed as a decree of a civil court. Appeals can be filed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
facts: The NGT is a statutory body established in 2010 under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010).
Objective: relief and compensation for environmental damage, polluter pays principle, and sustainable development.
India is the 3rd country after Australia and New Zealand to set up a specialised environmental tribunal.
The Chairperson is a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
Principal place of sitting is New Delhi, with regional benches at Kolkata, Bhopal, Pune and Chennai.
The NGT is mandated to dispose of appeals within 6 months of their filing.
Appeals can be filed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
The NGT is guided by principles of natural justice and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
The NGT excludes the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 from its jurisdiction.
NGT decisions are executable as a decree of a civil court.

subtopics.title: Scheme Overview and Need
subtopics.summary: The Cabinet approved the Samudra Manthan Scheme, a National Offshore Exploration Scheme to unlock India's offshore hydrocarbon potential. It is a Central Sector Scheme under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, focused on deepwater, ultra-deepwater and frontier offshore exploration. The case for it rests on high risks, long gestation periods and the natural decline of existing fields.
facts: Cabinet approved Samudra Manthan, a National Offshore Exploration Scheme.
The scheme aims to unlock India's offshore hydrocarbon potential.
It is a Central Sector Scheme under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Focus is on deepwater, ultra-deepwater and frontier offshore hydrocarbon exploration.
Offshore exploration involves high financial and technological risks.
Offshore projects have long gestation periods of around 5-10 years.
A deepwater exploratory well can cost approximately $125-150 million.
Existing oil and gas fields face natural production declines of around 6-7% annually.
Implementation period runs up to FY 2030-31.
keywords: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas

subtopics.title: Key Components and Targets
subtopics.summary: The scheme works through five components: seismic exploration, exploratory drilling, common infrastructure, manufacturing and services, and technology and capacity building. It sets production targets to add reserves, raise annual domestic output and expand the resource base. Priority is given to frontier and prospective offshore basins.
facts: Seismic exploration covers acquisition, processing and interpretation of seismic data.
Seismic work is used to identify prospective offshore hydrocarbon resources.
Exploratory drilling is accelerated in deepwater, ultra-deepwater and frontier offshore basins.
Common infrastructure means shared offshore production and evacuation infrastructure.
Common infrastructure aims to reduce costs and improve project viability.
Manufacturing and services: an integrated oil and gas manufacturing and services zone.
Technology and capacity building covers digital programme management, technology adoption, skill development, stakeholder engagement and international cooperation.
Target: add over 600 MMTOE of reserves.
Target: annual domestic oil and gas production from around 62 MMTOE to 80 MMTOE.
Target: expand resource base from around 1.6 billion to 2.2 billion tonnes of oil equivalent.
Priority basins include Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Mahanadi and the Andaman region.

subtopics.title: Financial Outlay and Risk-Sharing
subtopics.summary: The scheme has a total outlay of 84,084 crore, with separate allocations for exploratory wells, seismic data, infrastructure hubs and manufacturing zones. Government supports up to 50% of eligible drilling costs under a risk-sharing mechanism. This is designed to attract private investment into technically difficult offshore projects.
facts: Total outlay of the scheme is 84,084 crore.
The scheme is a Central Sector Scheme.
The allocation includes 60 deepwater exploratory wells.
Common Offshore Infrastructure Hubs receive 10,000 crore.
Oil and Gas Manufacturing and Services Zones receive 2,000 crore.
Risk-sharing: government supports up to 50% of eligible drilling costs.
Risk-sharing is meant to reduce the financial risk of offshore exploration.
Risk-sharing aims to encourage private and sustained investment.

subtopics.title: Significance for India
subtopics.summary: The scheme matters for energy security, because greater domestic production can reduce imports of crude oil and gas. Risk-sharing can make difficult offshore projects attractive to private investors. Indigenous technology and large-scale employment are also expected benefits.
facts: Greater domestic production can reduce India's dependence on imported crude oil and gas.
Government risk-sharing can make technically difficult offshore projects attractive to private investors.
Developing indigenous offshore technologies, equipment and services can reduce dependence on foreign capabilities.
The scheme supports the Atmanirbhar Bharat goal.
Large-scale exploration and associated infrastructure can generate skilled and supporting employment.

subtopics.title: Deep Ocean Mission and Matsya6000
subtopics.summary: The Deep Ocean Mission, run by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, includes the Samudrayaan mission to explore the ocean bed. Samudrayaan is a crewed expedition to 6,000 metres in the central Indian Ocean, using the Matsya6000 submersible. This programme is distinct from the Samudra Manthan Scheme.
facts: The Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) is spearheaded by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES).
DOM was approved in 2021 with a budget of Rs 4,077 crore over five years.
Samudrayaan is a key component of DOM and aims to explore the ocean bed.
Samudrayaan was launched in 2021 as India's flagship deep ocean mission.
It involves a crewed expedition to reach depths of 6,000 metres in the central Indian Ocean.
Matsya6000 is India's premier human submersible for deep-sea exploration.
Matsya6000 accommodates three aquanauts.
Operating endurance is 12 hours, expandable up to 96 hours in emergencies.
Matsya6000 is constructed from titanium alloy.
It travels at about 5.5 km/hr using underwater thrusters.

topics.title: Sarnath: India's 45th UNESCO World Heritage Site

subtopics.title: Inscription and India's World Heritage status
subtopics.summary: Sarnath was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee, held in Busan, Republic of Korea. With this inscription India has 45 World Heritage Sites, ranking 6th globally and 2nd in the Asia-Pacific region. Of these sites, 37 are cultural, 7 are natural and 1 is mixed.
facts: Inscribed during the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan (Republic of Korea)

India hosted the 46th Annual Session at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi
India served as a Committee Member for the 2021-2025 term

subtopics.title: Sarnath's sites and the first sermon
subtopics.summary: Sarnath is where Gautama Buddha gave his first sermon after attaining enlightenment at Bodhgaya, an event known as Dharmachakra Pravartana. The site has ancient names including Rishipatana, Ishipatana and Mrigadava. Its archaeological features include several stupas, a vihara and the Ashokan Pillar, each associated with a particular event or ruler.
facts: Ancient names: Rishipatana, Ishipatana and Mrigadava (Deer Park)
Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath after enlightenment at Bodhgaya

Dhamekh Stupa: marks the site of Buddha's first sermon
Dharmarajika Stupa: traditionally associated with Emperor Ashoka and Buddha's relics
Mulagandhakuti Vihara: Buddha's rainy-season retreat at Sarnath
Ashokan Pillar: erected during Ashoka's reign; its Lion Capital is India's National Emblem
Sarnath is one of 4 principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites (with Lumbini, Bodhgaya, Kushinagar)

subtopics.title: UNESCO, the Convention and the recognition process
subtopics.summary: The World Heritage List is maintained by the World Heritage Programme and administered by the UNESCO World Heritage Committee. The Convention concerning Protection of World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted in 1972, took effect in 1975, and was ratified by India in 1977. In India the Archaeological Survey of India is the nodal agency, while ICOMOS and IUCN carry out the assessment before the Committee takes the final decision.

UNESCO stands for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization

The list is administered by the UNESCO World Heritage Committee

India ratified the Convention in 1977
Nodal agency in India: Archaeological Survey of India

subtopics.title: Gautama Buddha and Buddhism
subtopics.summary: Gautama Buddha was born as Siddhartha in 563 BC at Lumbini, near Kapilavastu, and died at Kushinagara in 487 BC. He taught the Middle Path, the Four Noble Truths and the 8-Fold Path, and he called himself Tathagata. After his death his teachings were divided into three Pitakas at the First Buddhist Council.

Father was an elected ruler of Kapilvastu and headed the Shakya republican clan
Mother was a princess from the Koshalan dynasty
Death (Mahaparinirvana) at Kushinagara in 487 BC
Referred to himself as Tathagata (one who has thus come or gone)
Buddhism based on his teachings, developed in the 6th century BC
Buddhism rejects the authority of the Vedas and the concept of soul (atman)
Middle Path (Madhyam Marg): avoid the extremes
Four Noble Truths: suffering, its cause, its ending, and the path to ending it
8-Fold Path: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, mindfulness, effort, concentration

subtopics.title: UNCCD and COP17 at a Glance
subtopics.summary: The UNCCD is the principal legally binding framework on desertification, land degradation and drought, and it is one of three Rio Conventions. Its core objective is sustainable land management and achieving Land Degradation Neutrality by 2030. COP17 concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and Egypt will host COP 18 in 2028.
facts: Adopted on 17 June 1994, observed as World Day to Combat Desertification
Came into force in December 1996
Principal legally binding framework dealing specifically with desertification, land degradation and drought
Core objective: promote sustainable land management and achieve Land Degradation Neutrality by 2030
LDN: quantity and quality of land resources remain stable or improve to support ecosystem functions and services
LDN is linked with SDG Target 15.3
Conference of the Parties (COP) is the principal decision-making body of UNCCD
Membership: 197 Parties (196 countries plus the European Union)
COP17 concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, under the theme 'Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.'
Egypt will host UNCCD COP 18 in Sharm El-Sheikh in 2028

subtopics.title: Drought: Index, Facility and Treaty
subtopics.summary: Drought was a major focus at COP17, which saw a new Drought Resilience Index introduced to assess national preparedness. The Drought Resilience Investment Facility, launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg, uses public finance to attract private and institutional capital. Countries could not agree on a legally binding global drought agreement, and drought gets a standalone agenda item from COP 18 onwards.
facts: Drought Resilience Index: a comprehensive technical instrument for assessing national preparedness against drought
The index combines AI-based analytics, vulnerability assessment and risk mapping
Aim: shift drought management from post-disaster relief to anticipatory planning and resilience-building
Drought Resilience Investment Facility (DRIF) was launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg
DRIF uses public finance to de-risk investments and attract private and institutional capital
DRIF focuses on drought resilience, water security, climate-resilient agriculture and land restoration
Around USD 1.3 billion in new and pipeline funding was announced for land restoration and drought resilience in vulnerable countries
Countries could not reach consensus on a legally binding global agreement on drought
From COP 18 onwards, drought will receive a standalone agenda item

subtopics.title: Global Partnerships and Finance
subtopics.summary: The Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership, launched at COP 16 in 2024, initially secured around USD 2.15 billion and aims to support 80 countries. The Business4Land Initiative is UNCCD's major platform for private sector involvement in sustainable land management, water management and land restoration. COP17 also promoted nature-based solutions and ecosystem restoration in national development planning.
facts: Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership was launched during UNCCD COP 16 in Riyadh in 2024
The partnership initially secured around USD 2.15 billion in commitments
Its aim is to support 80 vulnerable and drought-affected countries through public and private finance
Business4Land Initiative is UNCCD's major platform for involving the private sector
Business4Land covers sustainable land management, water management and land restoration
COP17 promoted greater adoption of Nature-based Solutions
COP17 promoted Ecosystem-based Adaptation and Ecosystem Restoration in national development planning

Land degradation threatens ecosystems, agriculture, water availability and economic stability

subtopics.title: India's Position and National Programmes
subtopics.summary: India launched a Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems at COP17 to improve their recognition and conservation. Under the Bonn Challenge, India has brought around 21.76 million hectares of degraded and deforested land under restoration, against a broader target of 26 million hectares by 2030. Domestic programmes include the National Action Plan to Combat Desertification, the Green India Mission, Mission Amrit Sarovar and the Aravalli Green Wall Initiative.
facts: India is a Party to the UNCCD
India launched the Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) at COP17

Mission Amrit Sarovar focuses on creation and rejuvenation of water bodies; Aravalli Green Wall Initiative restores degraded Aravalli areas

topics.title: Global Tiger Day and Tiger Conservation

subtopics.title: Global Tiger Day and the TX2 Goal
subtopics.summary: Global Tiger Day is observed every year on 29 July and traces its origin to the 2010 St. Petersburg Tiger Summit in Russia. Thirteen Tiger Range Countries, including India, adopted the St. Petersburg Declaration. Their shared TX2 goal was to double the global wild tiger population by 2022.
facts: Observed annually on 29 July; the booklet credits IUCN with the observance

subtopics.title: Global Initiatives: IUCN, NTCA Eco-Tourism and IBCA
subtopics.summary: The IUCN Integrated Tiger Habitat Conservation Programme supports habitat restoration, anti-poaching measures and community-led coexistence across Asia. The NTCA Eco-Tourism Initiative provides an integrated platform for authentic safari and accommodation bookings. The International Big Cat Alliance, launched in 2023, is an India-led effort covering seven big cat species.
facts: IUCN programme supports habitat restoration, anti-poaching and community-led coexistence
The IUCN programme covers Asia
NTCA Eco-Tourism Initiative is an integrated platform for bookings

subtopics.title: Indian Institutions and Conservation Milestones
subtopics.summary: The National Board for Wild Life is a statutory board under the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972, and works to promote conservation of wildlife and forests. Project Tiger, launched in 1973, is overseen by the National Tiger Conservation Authority, which conducts the tiger census along with the Wildlife Institute of India. The milestones run from the 1969 ban on export of wild cat skins to the 2023 launch of the International Big Cat Alliance.

Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to support preservation of tigers in India
Project Tiger is overseen by the National Tiger Conservation Authority
Tiger census estimates population through a 4-year census cycle

2023: International Big Cat Alliance launched

subtopics.title: Tiger Reserves and Tiger Population in India
subtopics.summary: India has 58 Tiger Reserves, which are specially designated protected areas under Project Tiger and cover over 2.3 per cent of India's total land. Madhya Pradesh leads with the most reserves, and Corbett has the highest tiger abundance among them. India's tiger population was 3,682 in the 2022 figure, with Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka as the top states.

topics.title: Glaw Lake becomes India's 101st Ramsar Site

subtopics.title: Wetlands: Meaning and Types
subtopics.summary: A wetland is an area of land covered by water, whether salt, fresh or in between, either seasonally or permanently. Includes mangroves, coral reefs and other coastal areas

Segment 3: human-made wetlands

subtopics.title: Ramsar Convention and Montreux Record
subtopics.summary: The Ramsar Convention, formally the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance, is an intergovernmental treaty adopted in 1971 in Ramsar, Iran, and in force from 1975. subtopics.title: Government Initiatives to Preserve Wetlands
subtopics.summary: The Amrit Dharohar Capacity Building Scheme is a joint effort of the Ministry of Tourism and MoEFCC to make optimal use of wetlands. subtopics.title: Glasgow 2026 at a glance
subtopics.summary: The 23rd Commonwealth Games were held in Glasgow, Scotland, from 23 July to 2 August 2026, bringing together 74 nations and territories. subtopics.title: History and evolution of the Games

subtopics.title: India's medal performance at Glasgow 2026

subtopics.title: International Affairs and Places
subtopics.summary: This group covers a three-nation defence pact in West Asia, the NATO Ankara Summit 2026, the India-Bangladesh Ganga water sharing treaty and Nauru's new indigenous name. subtopics.title: Governance, Welfare and Digital Safety

subtopics.title: Environment, Energy and Wildlife

subtopics.title: History, Symbols and Personalities

quizzes.title: Ceuta: geography, status and disputes
quizzes.passage: Ceuta is a small Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa. It is bordered on its land side by a neighbouring state, and a strong fence separates the enclave from that country. Because of this position, the enclave has long been a point of concern for people who travel between the two continents. Many of those who arrive there are seeking work, education or a better life, while others are fleeing conflict or persecution in their home countries. Tensions over a distant territory add another layer to the story. Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony, has been the subject of a long dispute involving neighbouring countries and groups seeking self-determination. Changes in the relations between Spain and its neighbours have, at different times, affected how many people reach the enclave. Officials therefore treat the border not as a purely local matter but as part of a wider regional pattern. Ceuta's story shows how geography and politics can combine. A place that is small on the map can become a major point of diplomacy when large numbers of people try to cross into it. Resolving such moments usually depends on cooperation between governments, as well as on the legal rules that protect people who seek safety. Such episodes also test how well the rules protecting people who seek safety are applied in practice.

quizzes.title: Refugee and trafficking treaties
quizzes.passage: International law on refugees and trafficking is built from several separate agreements rather than one document. Some agreements focus on organised crime and on protecting people, especially women and children, from being exploited. Others define who counts as a refugee, what rights that person should have, and why a refugee must not be sent back to a place of danger. Still other treaties cover civil and political rights, and they include protections against cruel treatment when a person is returned to their home country. The framework also reaches children, whose welfare in conflict and displacement is addressed by a separate treaty on their rights. Several newer initiatives support host communities that receive large numbers of refugees, and they encourage countries to share responsibility. Governments may meet at regular intervals to review progress on refugee issues. Not every country has joined the main refugee agreements, and this affects how such countries treat people who arrive seeking protection. Each agreement was written for a different purpose, so their scope and obligations vary. Overall, the system combines criminal law, human rights and humanitarian commitments into one broad structure.

quizzes.title: Claims, Law and Disputes
quizzes.passage:
The South China Sea has been a focus of competing territorial claims for many decades. Several countries around its shores assert rights over islands, reefs and surrounding waters, and their claims often overlap. The sea is also rich in resources and fishing grounds, which gives every claimant a practical reason to hold on to the features it controls.

After the Second World War, islands that Japanese forces had used for military purposes became part of the wider question of ownership. Claims were soon drawn on maps, and China's claim is commonly described through a boundary line marked on official maps. That line continued to appear on official maps even after the Chinese Communist Party came to power, and it covers a large share of the sea.

A United Nations convention on the law of the sea sets a legal framework that tries to balance the interests of coastal states and seafaring nations. Although the countries involved have signed and ratified it, its interpretation in this sea remains fiercely disputed. In the early 2000s, ASEAN and China agreed on a declaration meant to manage and resolve disputes.

Disputes have also gone to international bodies. The Philippines brought its case to an arbitral tribunal, arguing that China's claims violated its sovereignty. The tribunal ruled against China, which rejected the ruling and said it preferred bilateral negotiations with the other parties involved. Overlapping claims continue to shape naval activity, fishing and access to resources in the region.

quizzes.title: Antelope Reef Facts
quizzes.passage:
Antelope Reef has moved to the centre of debate over military activity in the South China Sea. The reef lies in a group of islands where several states have competing claims, and the area is among the busiest maritime zones in the world. Shipping that carries a large share of global trade moves through these waters every year, so any change in the region draws close attention from neighbouring countries and from trading nations far away.

Reports describe construction work that has transformed the reef, with reclaimed land, a wharf and other port facilities built alongside. Such facilities are often linked to naval use, but the government that controls the site has described its work differently and has pointed to scientific research. The reef could support larger operations over time.

Security experts have discussed what such a base could mean for the wider balance of power. A secure base for large submarines would be valuable to any navy, and a well-equipped reef could also support surveillance and patrols. Neighbouring countries have reason for concern, since military facilities on disputed features could change how the sea is used and who controls its routes.

Questions for the region now include how these developments fit into a broader plan to strengthen maritime influence, and whether other states will respond with their own installations.

quizzes.title: Selection process and straw polls
quizzes.passage: The United Nations Security Council has held a second round of informal straw polls to help identify a successor to Antonio Guterres, whose second term as Secretary-General is due to end at the close of the year. The selection process begins when the presidents of the General Assembly and the Security Council jointly write to member states, inviting them to put forward candidates. Nominees usually submit a curriculum vitae and a vision statement describing their experience and qualifications. They then take part in interactive dialogues, where they explain their plans for the organisation and answer questions. The straw poll is the next stage. It is an informal and confidential exercise in which Council members show how acceptable each candidate is to them. Because the process runs through successive rounds, weaker candidates can be filtered out over time. Each round gives the Council a clearer picture of which names have broad acceptance among its members, and the process is designed to continue until one candidate has the backing needed. The straw polls are an important stage in narrowing the field, but they are not the final step, since the Council must still formally recommend a candidate before the General Assembly acts.

quizzes.title: Term, appointment and rotation
quizzes.passage: The selection of the UN Secretary-General combines written rules with long-standing custom. The founding Charter explains how the post is filled, but it does not set a limit on how long the holder may serve. Over time, a standard length of office has developed through practice, and the holder is normally allowed to seek a further term, although this rests on custom rather than written rules. The Security Council plays the decisive role in the process. The Council has fifteen members, and each one holds a single vote, so its recommendation reflects collective judgment rather than the preference of one state. When the Council settles on a candidate, its recommendation passes to the wider membership of the United Nations, which makes the formal appointment. Even though that wider body could decide by a simple majority, appointments have usually been made without a vote, through agreement or general approval. The choice is also shaped by an unwritten expectation that the post should move between different parts of the world. This expectation is meant to give every region a fair chance of representation at the top of the organisation. Candidates are expected to present their experience and their vision for the organisation before member states, so that the process is open and transparent. The practice is widely followed among members, and it reflects an effort to balance representation across the world.

quizzes.title: Cauvery dispute history check
quizzes.passage: The Cauvery water dispute is one of the oldest inter-state water conflicts in India, and its roots lie in agreements made long before independence. The disagreement began between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore. Madras objected when Mysore planned to expand its irrigation and build new water storage structures on the river. A later arrangement allowed Mysore to construct a dam at a village in the region, and that dam later became a major reservoir. The original agreement was meant to operate for a fixed period, and when it came up for review, it became a major source of contention between the successor states. The upper riparian state wants more water for Bengaluru's drinking water and irrigation, while the lower riparian state wants assured releases to support the agriculture of its delta. Because the states could not settle the matter by agreement, the dispute was taken up under the legal framework available for such conflicts. A tribunal was then formed to decide the sharing of water, and its award was later examined by the Supreme Court. Today, a statutory body works to put the final decision into practice, with the help of a regulation committee. Current releases and new projects such as Mekedatu keep the dispute active in public debate.

quizzes.title: Historical Roots and Current Process
quizzes.passage: The demand for a separate political or administrative arrangement for the Nepali-speaking Gorkha population of the Darjeeling Hills in West Bengal has a long history. The Gorkhas are people of Nepali origin, and the term is linked to the historic Gorkha Kingdom of Western Nepal. Political demands for greater autonomy can be traced to the early twentieth century, when the Darjeeling Hillmen's Association petitioned during the Minto-Morley Reforms. Other organisations, including the Gorkha Officers' Association, kept raising demands for greater political autonomy in the years that followed. The Gorkhas also have a distinctive martial tradition, and the British began systematic recruitment of Gorkha soldiers after the Anglo-Nepal War. The movement became far more intense during the 1980s under a new political force. Over time, the movement's objective became clearer in its articulation. More recently, the Ministry of Home Affairs convened a Tripartite Meeting involving the Government of West Bengal and representatives of the Gorkha community. Following that meeting, the Union Government constituted a committee to work out modalities for a Permanent Political Solution. quizzes.title: Institutions and Challenges Recall
quizzes.passage: Successive arrangements have tried to give the Darjeeling hill region a measure of self-governance since the agitation of the 1980s. quizzes.passage: Parliament has passed the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026. The amendment follows the controversy over the NEET-UG 2024 paper leak, in which alleged leak networks were reported to be operating in Patna (Bihar) and Hazaribagh (Jharkhand). Concern grew after 67 candidates secured full marks, aided by disputed grace marks, which triggered nationwide protests and judicial scrutiny. Earlier, Parliament had enacted the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024. It is India's first dedicated central legislation on question-paper leaks, organised cheating and examination-related fraud. The Act covers major examinations conducted by bodies such as the UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, the National Testing Agency and the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection. The 2026 Amendment is aimed at stronger deterrence. It revises the penalties under four categories: individual offences, service providers, organised examination crime and organised crimes. The penalty for each category differs, so the consequence depends on the category of offence. Demands for stronger deterrence and faster legal proceedings also grew as the controversy continued. The amendment also aims to ensure that examination fraud cases do not remain pending for prolonged periods. It introduces time-bound investigation and trial for offences under the Act. The revised penalties apply to offences under the Act, which covers the examinations listed above.

India protects its national symbols through specific laws. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, is the main law that deals with deliberate insults to the national emblems. It covers the National Flag, the Constitution and the National Anthem, Jana Gana Mana, and it makes certain acts against them punishable. The law describes acts such as burning, defacing or desecrating the flag, and it also covers preventing people from singing the anthem or disturbing a gathering while it is sung. The Act has three main provisions, dealing with the flag and Constitution, the anthem, and repeat offences. The Act was later strengthened so that people who repeat such offences face stricter treatment.

In 2026, the Central Government proposed an amendment to this law in the Rajya Sabha. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, aims to extend statutory protection to Vande Mataram, a patriotic song. Under the proposal, intentionally insulting Vande Mataram would become a punishable offence. At present, the Act protects the flag, the Constitution and the anthem, while the amendment seeks to include the National Song, Vande Mataram, within this legal framework. quizzes.title: Vande Mataram history: recall
quizzes.passage:
Vande Mataram is a patriotic song written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. It was composed as a response to British promotion of 'God Save the King', and it first appeared in a magazine in 1875. Later, the song became part of a novel in which warrior-monks sing it. The song praises Mother India through the image of a goddess, and its verses are divided into stanzas, with some verses in Sanskrit and the rest in Bengali.

After the Partition of Bengal in 1905, the song became closely linked with the national struggle. It was sung in public for the first time at Town Hall in Calcutta, and it soon became the customary opening song at a Congress session. An Indian flag bearing its words was also unfurled in Europe. Several tunes were composed for the song over the years, and it was sung at many national events.

Later, the national leadership had to decide how much of the song should be used at gatherings. After independence, the song was declared the National Song of India and was to be honoured equally with the National Anthem. The Constitution does not explicitly recognise a National Song. Its popularity and its official status therefore developed over several decades.

quizzes.title: National Tribunals Commission: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage: The Lok Sabha has passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026, which proposes to establish a National Tribunals Commission for unified governance of tribunals. The Bill is intended to replace the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and to restructure the legal framework that governs tribunal appointments and service conditions. It also re-enacts provisions of the 2021 law that were struck down, and it is drafted in line with the Supreme Court's directions on judicial independence and separation of powers. The Supreme Court has repeatedly examined provisions that gave the Executive excessive control over tribunals, including in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India. The proposed Commission would provide a common institutional framework for all tribunals covered under the Bill. Its major functions include selecting tribunal chairpersons and members, reviewing the performance of members, overseeing complaints and disciplinary inquiries, and providing administrative supervision. It will also maintain a national tribunals data grid. For selection, a Search-cum-Selection Committee will recommend candidates for each vacancy. The Commission framework applies to a wide range of bodies, from central and state administrative tribunals to specialised bodies such as the Armed Forces Tribunal and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. The Central Government will frame the rules governing service conditions. Reappointment for another term is considered on the basis of past performance.

quizzes.title: National Green Tribunal: typed answer practice
quizzes.passage: The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body created under an Act of Parliament to deal with environmental disputes. Its objective is to provide relief and compensation for environmental damage, and its work rests on the polluter pays principle and the goal of sustainable development. India is one of the few countries to have set up a specialised environmental tribunal, and the NGT is the body through which such cases are heard. The Tribunal is headed by a Chairperson who is either a retired Supreme Court judge or a former Chief Justice of a High Court. Its members are of two kinds, judicial members and expert members, and the Central Government decides their exact number. The Tribunal has a principal place of sitting and also holds sittings at regional benches in several other cities. The NGT hears civil cases arising under a set of environmental laws, and it has original jurisdiction over civil cases with substantial environmental questions. It is guided by the principles of natural justice and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure. Its decisions can be executed as a decree of a civil court. Appeals against its orders can be taken to the Supreme Court, and the Tribunal must dispose of appeals within a fixed period from the date they are filed. Certain statutes, including a wildlife law and a forest rights law, are excluded from its jurisdiction.

quizzes.title: Components, targets and priority basins
quizzes.passage:
India imports a large part of the crude oil and natural gas it uses, and policymakers have long wanted more of this supply to come from within the country. Much of the unexplored potential lies beneath the sea, in deep and far-off waters where drilling is costly and technically demanding. Companies hesitate to commit money to such projects because results can take years to arrive, and an exploratory well that finds nothing is an expensive loss. At the same time, the fields that already produce oil and gas do not stay productive forever. Their output falls every year as the reservoirs age, so new discoveries are needed just to keep production steady.

The Samudra Manthan Scheme is the government's response to this problem. It is built around several linked streams of work. Some streams focus on locating resources and on drilling in difficult waters. Others focus on shared facilities that can move produced oil and gas, on building a domestic base of manufacturing and services, and on developing skills and technology. The plan also sets a clear quantity goal, aiming to add a large volume of reserves and to raise annual domestic output. Taken together, the scheme hopes to reduce risk for investors, strengthen national capability, and make India less reliant on imported energy in the years ahead.

quizzes.title: Outlay and risk-sharing
quizzes.passage:
Offshore hydrocarbon exploration needs large sums of public money before any oil or gas reaches the market. Surveys of the seabed, test drilling in deep water and the construction of shared facilities all require heavy spending. The government has therefore set aside a fixed amount for the scheme for a defined period. The money is divided among several heads, covering drilling, data collection, common infrastructure and manufacturing zones. Some of these heads are large and others are small, reflecting their different roles.

The government has also chosen to share part of the cost of drilling with companies that take part. This is meant to lower the financial risk that makes private firms hesitant about offshore work. Because the sharing applies only to eligible costs, the rules define which expenses qualify. Officials expect that the combination of public allocations and shared risk will encourage firms to commit capital and bring technology to difficult frontier areas. The scheme's funding is therefore a central feature of its design, and its long-term success depends on steady investment across all of these heads.

quizzes.title: Sarnath: inscription, sites and sermon
quizzes.passage: Sarnath, a Buddhist site in Uttar Pradesh, has recently been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The inscription was made at a meeting of the World Heritage Committee, and it raised the total number of such sites in India. Sarnath holds a special place in Buddhist history because Gautama Buddha gave his first teaching there after attaining enlightenment at Bodhgaya. The event marks the beginning of the Buddhist monastic community, known as the Sangha, and it is linked with the Noble Eightfold Path. The site was known in earlier times by several names, and it is visited today for its monuments. Visitors see the Chaukhandi, Dhamekh and Dharmarajika stupas, a vihara and the Ashokan Pillar. Many of these structures are linked with episodes from the Buddha's life or with rulers of the past. Sarnath is also counted among the principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites, which draw devotees from many countries. India has many heritage sites of different kinds, grouped as cultural, natural and mixed. Each category holds its own set of monuments, and together they show how varied the country's heritage is. The process of recognition involves assessment by expert bodies before the final decision is taken by the committee. Such a listing is a major achievement for any country, because it brings the monument to the attention of the whole world.

quizzes.title: Buddha's life and Buddhist teachings
quizzes.passage: Gautama Buddha was born as Siddhartha in a noble family near Kapilavastu, close to Lumbini in present-day Nepal. His father was an elected ruler, and his mother came from a royal dynasty of Kosala. Siddhartha left his home in a famous departure and later attained enlightenment, after which people began to call him the Buddha. He spent the rest of his life teaching, and his first sermon was delivered at Sarnath. Buddhism, which developed on the basis of his teachings in the sixth century BC, emphasises the attainment of enlightenment and recommends following a middle path between extremes. Its followers reject the authority of the Vedas and the idea of a permanent soul, which sets Buddhism apart from some other traditions. After the Buddha passed away, his teachings were recited and organised at a series of gatherings known as councils. The first council grouped the teachings into collections, which were later written down. Buddhist texts preserve these teachings in several collections, including the main discourses and the rules of conduct for monks and nuns. The core of his message concerns suffering, its causes, its ending and the path that leads to that ending, and this remains central to the faith. Each of these ideas connects with the others, and together they form the basis of the religion.

quizzes.title: UNCCD and COP17 Recall
quizzes.passage: The 17th round of talks under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification recently concluded in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia. The meeting coincided with a United Nations observance that draws attention to pastoral communities and the management of rangelands, which are grasslands and open lands used for grazing. The emphasis on pastoral communities reflects how directly their livelihoods depend on the condition of the land. Land degradation was a central concern. It is described as a serious threat to ecosystems, farming, the availability of water and the economic stability of many regions. The crisis affects a large share of the world's land, and delegates argued that restoring whole landscapes is more effective than scattered, isolated projects. Mongolia used the platform to explain the severity of its own problem, and it has a national campaign to plant trees over the coming years. Several countries also promoted nature-based solutions and ecosystem restoration as part of national development planning. The convention itself is a legally binding framework dealing with desertification, land degradation and drought, and its work connects closely with climate and biodiversity agreements. Its broader aim is sustainable land management, so that land continues to support people and nature. Organisers and participants generally treated the conference as an opportunity to move from commitments on paper to restoration on the ground.

quizzes.title: Drought Policy Recall
quizzes.passage: Drought is one of the harder environmental problems to manage, because its damage builds slowly and is often noticed only after crops have failed and water supplies have run low. For a long time, the usual response has been relief once the harm is done. A newer approach asks governments to look at how exposed they are before the damage occurs. To support this, a comprehensive technical instrument was introduced to help countries judge how prepared they are for drought. It draws on modern data-analysis tools, studies the vulnerability of communities and maps the risks they face. Money is the other side of the problem. Public funds can play a catalytic role, bringing in private and institutional investors to finance water security, climate-resilient farming and land restoration. A fresh pool of finance announced at the recent conference was meant for restoring land and building drought resilience in vulnerable countries. Discussions about a binding global instrument for drought form part of the wider debate. Land and water are closely linked, so a drought in one region can quickly affect farming, food supplies and local incomes across wider areas. Pressure on water, farming and land tends to show up in the others as well. Overall, drought is best understood as a problem of preparation and investment, not only of emergency response.

quizzes.title: Global Tiger Day MCQ set
quizzes.passage: Wild tigers live in a number of countries across Asia, and Global Tiger Day is an occasion to focus attention on their survival. Governments and conservation groups treat the animal as a shared responsibility, because a tiger that roams across borders cannot be protected by one country alone. The international effort is organised around the countries where wild tigers still live, which are called Tiger Range Countries. These nations meet in summits and sign common documents that describe their aims. The programmes described for this region cover habitat restoration, measures against poaching and cooperation with local communities who live close to forests. A central idea in recent observances is coexistence, meaning that people and tigers should be able to share the same landscape. The campaign also stresses that solutions must be scaled up so that they reach many forests, not only a few protected areas. In India, the tiger is the national animal, and the country has a legal framework that governs how tiger reserves are created and protected. Public awareness is therefore as important as government action, since many tiger habitats are shared with local communities. Together, these efforts show that the future of the tiger depends on policy, science and the daily choices of people who share its habitat.

quizzes.title: Tiger reserves TITA set
quizzes.passage: Tiger reserves are protected areas that receive a special status so that tigers can breed, move and live without constant disturbance. In India, these areas are created under a national programme that gives them legal backing and dedicated management. Any change to a reserve's boundaries needs careful approval, because the rules are meant to protect the animals within them. Officials therefore treat reserve notification as a formal process, not a routine administrative step. Tiger reserves vary greatly in size, from small forest patches to very large landscapes that cover several districts. Their tiger numbers are estimated through a periodic count carried out by official agencies with the help of research institutes. Counting takes place in fixed cycles, so that results from different years can be compared. Some states have many reserves while others have only a few. Software-based monitoring systems help managers track conditions in these reserves and respond to threats. Local communities also play a role, because conservation in and around forests depends on people living alongside wildlife. The scale of this work is large, and even small changes in reserve boundaries can affect many animals. Together, these features explain why tiger reserves remain central to the country's conservation strategy.

quizzes.title: Glaw Lake and Ramsar Basics
quizzes.passage: Glaw Lake, a lake in the Eastern Himalayas, has recently gained recognition as a wetland of global importance. It lies in Arunachal Pradesh, a state in north-eastern India, and its waters are fresh rather than salty. The lake sits within a protected area. The recognition came under the Ramsar Convention, the intergovernmental treaty on wetlands. It is the only international treaty that addresses one specific ecosystem. Under this treaty, wetlands of international importance are declared as Ramsar sites. The term wetland is broad. It describes any area of land covered by water, whether that water is salt, fresh or somewhere in between, and whether it is present seasonally or permanently. Wetland types include rivers, swamps, wet grasslands, peatlands, deltas and tidal flats, as well as mangroves and coral reefs. The treaty has been in force for decades and has many member states. Glaw Lake's recognition is an example of a wider expansion of India's protected wetlands network. India has steadily added sites to its Ramsar network over the years. India also runs a National Wetland Conservation Program, implemented through state authorities. Government schemes also support this work. One scheme focuses on the optimal use of wetlands, and its aims include enhancing biodiversity, carbon stock and income for local communities. Another focus is moving from high-volume tourism to nature tourism at ecologically sensitive wetlands.

quizzes.title: Wetland Policy Tools
quizzes.passage: Protecting wetlands in India involves policy as well as science, and several central initiatives work through states and cities. One is a capacity building scheme run jointly by two ministries. Its aim is to encourage the optimal use of wetlands while enhancing biodiversity, carbon stock and eco-tourism. The scheme also seeks to generate income for local communities. Local communities are among the intended beneficiaries of the scheme. A second measure is the National Wetland Conservation Program, which is carried out through State Wetland Authorities. Later, a regulatory framework for wetlands was notified under a major environmental law. This framework decentralises wetland management and provides for State or Union Territory Wetlands Authorities. Cities can also be recognised for wetland care. The Wetland City Accreditation Program is part of the Ramsar Convention. The Wetland City Accreditation Program promotes the conservation and wise use of urban and peri-urban wetlands. Accreditation is granted only to cities that satisfy all of the programme's international criteria. Protection is also linked with tourism. The government has announced a Nature-Culture Tourism Corridor in Uttar Pradesh, to be developed between two places. Mapping supports these efforts too. A national atlas of wetland decadal change, prepared by a national agency, tracks how wetlands have changed over time. Taken together, these steps reflect a move toward careful use of sensitive wetlands.

quizzes.title: History of the Games: short answers
quizzes.passage:

The event was generally held once every four years, although the editions scheduled for 1942 and 1946 did not take place.

Today the Games are organised by the Commonwealth Games Federation, and each edition is hosted by a nation chosen in advance. India has hosted the Games, and its best performance at the Games, with 101 medals, came at that edition.

A centenary edition of the Games is planned for India in a future year, which will mark one hundred years since the first Games. India's first participation came decades before it hosted the Games, showing a long link with the event. quizzes.title: Flag, freedom and the navy
quizzes.passage:
The national flag of India took shape over several decades of the freedom struggle. Pingali Venkayya, a freedom fighter from Andhra Pradesh, worked on flag designs and is remembered for his role in the Indian Tricolour. At the 1921 session of the Indian National Congress held at Vijayawada, he presented a khadi flag design to Mahatma Gandhi. His first design had red and green bands, with a charkha at the centre, representing the two major communities. On Gandhi's suggestion, a white band was added to stand for peace, while the charkha was kept as a symbol of self-reliance. In 1931, the Congress formally adopted a modified tricolour, which became the precursor of the present flag. The Constituent Assembly adopted the present National Flag on 22 July 1947, and it became the national flag of independent India on 15 August 1947.

The freedom movement also reached the armed forces. In 1946, Indian naval ratings rose against British authorities in several port cities, demanding better food, pay comparable with the Royal Navy, and an end to the use of Indian personnel for British imperial expansion. The uprising drew support from workers, students and civilians. Its anti-colonial mood was shaped in part by the legacy of the Indian National Army trials.

Symbols and protests of this period show how closely ideas of unity, peace and self-reliance were linked with the struggle for independence.
